title: Tell a many-to-many relation from a one-value function
sources: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.1200J Mathematics for Computer Science, Lecture 15: Relations and Counting (Spring 2024)
Python 3.14.8 Built-in Types: set and dict concepts
masterChecklist: Discrete-math essentials: logic, sets, relations, functions, induction, counting, probability, modular arithmetic
whyItMatters: A data model can accidentally discard valid records if a many-to-many relationship is stored in a one-value dictionary. Conversely, a feature that requires exactly one current value per learner needs explicit validation.
simpleExplanation: A relation between learners and lessons is a set of ordered pairs. One learner may appear with several lessons. A function from learners to current lessons permits at most one current lesson for each learner; a total function also assigns one to every learner in its declared domain. In Python, a set of `(learner, lesson)` tuples can represent the relation, while a dictionary can represent a single-value mapping. Repeated dictionary assignment to the same key replaces the old value, so validate whether multiple values are allowed before choosing the structure.
mentalModel: A library checkout log can show one reader borrowing several books. A 'current desk number' map gives each present reader one desk. Forcing the checkout log into a one-desk map loses books.
outcomes: Describe a relation as ordered pairs.
Distinguish one-to-many data from a total single-value mapping.
Reject conflicting values when a one-value contract is required.
Check domain coverage rather than assuming a dictionary is total.

realWorldExample.scenario: A study app stores every learner-to-completed-lesson pair, plus exactly one current lesson per active learner.
realWorldExample.riskWithoutSetup: Code writes completed pairs to a dict keyed only by learner and silently keeps just the last completion. A separate current-lesson dict may omit an active learner without detection.
realWorldExample.professionalApproach: Keep completions as a relation, represented by pairs or a relational table; validate the active-learner current mapping for no conflicts and full domain coverage.

explanation: completed is a relation: Ada appears in two distinct learner/lesson pairs without losing either.
current_pairs is intended to become a total function over the active domain.
A conflicting second value for one learner is rejected before dictionary assignment could silently replace the first.
The final set comparison checks that every active learner has a current lesson; a dict alone would not guarantee coverage.
The example permits a duplicate identical pair, which does not change the single-value mapping. A production model may choose to reject duplicate records separately.
workedExample.safeExperiment: Add ('Ada', 'Files') to current_pairs and predict the error. Then remove Bo's pair and predict the other error.

procedure: Write down the domain and codomain of the feature.
Ask whether one input can legitimately relate to more than one output.
Use a relation of pairs for many-to-many data; do not flatten it into a single-value dict.
For a one-value mapping, reject conflicting outputs for the same input.
If the function must be total, check that every domain member is mapped.
Test one-to-many, conflicting, missing and unknown-domain cases.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing `mapping[learner] = lesson` for every completion row.
commonMistakes.why: Later lessons replace earlier values for the same learner.
commonMistakes.avoid: Keep completion pairs in a relation or group them into collections.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling any dictionary a total function over all learners.
commonMistakes.why: Some declared learners may be absent.
commonMistakes.avoid: Compare its keys with the required domain.

commonMistakes.why: (learner, lesson) and (lesson, learner) model different relationships.
commonMistakes.avoid: Name the domain and codomain and use consistent tuple positions.

lab.title: Validate one current lesson per active learner
lab.safety: Only fictional in-memory strings are used. Run the exercise in the site's bundled Python worker.
lab.starterCode:
def current_map(domain, pairs):
    # Reject unknown learners, conflicting lessons, and missing learners.
    pass

# Test valid, conflict, missing and unknown cases.
guidedSteps: Reject a pair whose learner is not in domain.
Reject a different lesson for a learner already present.
After all pairs, compare result keys with the full domain.
Test a valid map and each of the three invalid cases.
checks: Valid mapping contains one value for every domain member.
Conflicting value is rejected, not silently overwritten.
hints: Check `learner in result and result[learner] != lesson` before assignment.
lab.solutionExplanation: The function enforces at-most-one output through the conflict check and exactly-one-for-every-domain-member through the final coverage check. Completions that allow several lessons should not use this structure.
challenges: Predict whether two identical Ada/Loops pairs pass.
Find the bug: assign to the dict before checking a conflict.
Experiment: represent completed lessons with a set of pairs instead of this dict.

simulation.prompt: Ada completed Input and Loops. Is a dict mapping Ada to one lesson a lossless representation of both completions?
choices: No; a set of pairs or grouped collection is needed
simulation.explanation: A dictionary has one value per key, so a later assignment replaces the earlier one.

projectConnection.milestone: Store completed learner/lesson pairs without loss, and separately validate the one-current-lesson mapping for active learners.
projectConnection.definitionOfDone: One-to-many completions survive, conflicting current lessons fail, and every active learner has a current lesson.

assessment.question: Can a relation contain both (Ada, Input) and (Ada, Loops)?
assessment.explanation: A relation can have several ordered pairs with the same first component.

assessment.question: What makes a mapping total over a declared domain?
assessment.answer: Every domain member has exactly one output.

assessment.question: Why can a dictionary lose completion history?
assessment.answer: Assigning a new value to an existing learner key replaces the old value.
assessment.explanation: Use a relation or a collection of values when several outputs are valid.
